en: Preface to the Ox-Herding Pictures:
The *Śālistamba-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Bequeathed Teachings) states: "It is like herding oxen; one must hold the staff and watch them so that they do not run wild and trespass upon the crops.
This is the origin of the discourse on herding oxen. Following this, Mazu asked Shigong: "What are you doing here?"
[The Master] asked, "What is your occupation? He replied, "I herd oxen. [The Master] asked again, "How do you herd oxen? He replied, "Once they have gone into the grass, I pull them back by the nose.
This is what it means to be a skilled herder. Furthermore, when Master Daowu An was at Mount Miao...
He said, "I dwell at Mount Gui, yet I do not study the Chan of Mount Gui; I simply herd a single water buffalo.
Furthermore, when Master Baiyun Cundao questioned Guo Gongfu, he asked, "Is the ox pure? Do you herd it yourself, or do you have another herd it?
These instances, appearing one after another throughout antiquity and the present, are increasingly clear and manifest. Later, there were even those who depicted them in painting.
The *Hutu* (Diagram) begins with Weimù and ends with the dual extinction (*shuangmin*). These are categorized and arranged into ten stages; as for the oxen, they follow the sequence:
first black, then white, continuing until nothingness. They appear vividly clear. Furthermore, Puming has appended a verse to each one.
As for Puming, it is not detailed where he was from. It is also unknown whether the diagram and the verses were produced by a single hand.

Setting aside other matters for now, consider only this: as for its diagrams, the imagery is manifest while the meaning is profound; as for its hymns, the words are near at hand while the intent is far-reaching.
Students hold them as a left-hand voucher (a guarantee), by means of which they examine virtue and investigate their practice, looking downward to observe what has already been attained.
I look up to what has not yet been reached, so as to avoid being satisfied with a mere trifle and falling into the stage of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This would be of great benefit; thus, I have recorded this and re-carved it for publication. Furthermore, there is the account of searching for the ox until finally entering the marketplace.
There are also ten diagrams, which are largely the same as those currently in use but with minor differences.
Furthermore, the sequential stages of cultivation and progress within the teachings—which may be understood by analogy—are all appended to these final pages for convenient reference.

As for those practitioners who enter directly and transcend all at once, they require no laborious urging or guidance; they are like the naturally manifest white ox on the open ground, transcending all hierarchical stages in an instant.
When both subject and object are simultaneously transcended, then diagrams become stagnant goods and verses become redundant speech; upon reading this, one should let out a laugh.
I have no further arguments to offer.
Written on the birthday of the Tathāgata in the Jiyou year of the Wanli era by the junior student Zuhong. Respectfully inscribed.
Preface to the Verses on the Ox-Herding Pictures of Puming Monastery:
*Tou!* The entire earth is the single ox of Puming. Where else could there be Buddhas or sentient beings?
There is not even a hair’s breadth of separation; it is fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*). If you say this ox is black or white, male or female, hungry...

To have satiety is precisely for one body to be differentiated into two. When the World-Honored One was first born, he pointed to heaven and pointed to earth; he walked seven steps and looked around in all directions.
[The people] did not fail to violate his crops by the few. When the Patriarch came from the West, he directly pointed to the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature, one becomes a Buddha.
He has consumed a great deal of their water and grass—the Three Essentials of the Mysteries, the Four Selections, the Five Ranks of Ruler and Subject, and the ninety-six circular diagrams.

Having endured all the constraints and goads, even the raising of the mallet, the brandishing of the whisk, the striking with the staff, and the shouting—these various functional devices have caused his skin and hair to fall away and his four hooves to vanish from sight. This large ox does not know where it has fled.
He has gone. Having arrived here, the heavy barrier has been broken. But tell me: is there still something further above? [The Master] strikes a circle with his whisk and says:
"A wooden ox plows through the white snow in the fire; a stone horse dances in the spring breeze amidst the clouds. Do you understand?
If not, please look at the *Oxherding Songs* and the verses composed in successive rhyme by various masters. Ultimately, which one is superior?
Even the inferior have none.
A humble preface by the Chan practitioner Yan Daceng, the thirty-second generation successor in the orthodox lineage of Linji,
respectfully composed as a preface to Master Puming’s *Verses on the Diagram of Tending the Ox*, with appended verses by various great Chan masters.
Preface to the Publication of the *Puming Yunsong* (The Original Verses of Puming) by the Great Master Yunqi Lianchi: "Puming is unknown as to where he was from, nor is his place of practice known.
In the winter of the year of Xinchou, I came to manage the affairs of this monastery; in the summer of the year of Renyin..."
The layman Che-do showed me the *nidāna* concerning the origins of Puyong-sa and an old map of the temple complex. Only then did I realize that the causal conditions for this site lay therein.
Once the layman had restored the temple foundations, he first invited the Chan Master Hyonwi, followed by the venerable elder Myeongnyang;

thus, the halls and buildings were resplendent and the quarters were fully provided. With the intention of eventually establishing a "lion’s den," I observed the harmony among the practitioners from various quarters.

Verse: Reading this, I am overcome with joy and exuberance; I have imitated its style to compose a response. I shall combine the original verses, the illustrations, and my response into a single volume for circulation.

Recorded by Renkong Ruzhenji on a day in the first month of autumn in the first year of the Kangxi era (1662), while residing at the Prajñā Hall. This is a commentary on the "Diagram of Herding the Ox" composed by the monk Mugong (also known as Chan Master Juche; his name was Guangyin, his style name Wengu), a man of the Way who relies on nothing. [Also appended: the "Ode to the White Ox. **The Monk Mugong’s Ode on the Diagram of Herding the Ox** **Verse One: Seeking the Ox** Seeking the ox, I roam through mountains and fields; My body is exhausted, yet my mind is not weary. I do not know where the ox has gone; Only the tracks remain upon the path. **Verse Two: Seeing the Tracks** Seeing the tracks, I know the ox is near; I follow them with all my heart and soul. Though the tracks are long and winding, They lead directly back to the homestead. **Verse Three: Seeing the Ox** Seeing the ox, I am filled with joy; Its horns are white, its tail is black. It grazes freely among the green hills; I have finally found it. **Verse Four: Catching the Ox** Catching the ox, I bind it with a rope; Day and night, I watch over it. Even if it breaks free and wanders afar, I will surely bring it back home. **Verse Five: Taming the Ox** Taming the ox, I apply the whip; It is difficult to subdue, yet I persevere. If it runs wild and acts recklessly, I must strike it with the stick. **Verse Six: Controlling the Ox** Controlling the ox, I hold the reins; It is like a wild horse that must be broken. When it roams the plains and marshes, I pull it back toward the mountain peaks. **Verse Seven: The Ox Lost** The ox is lost, and I am distraught; I search for it in every direction. If I do not find it soon, I fear I shall lose my way. **Verse Eight: The Ox Found** The ox is found, and I am at ease; I lead it back to the stable. I tie it securely to the hitching post; From now on, there is no more wandering. **Verse Nine: The Ox Transformed** The ox is transformed, and I am content; It no longer knows the ways of the world. It eats grass and drinks water at will; It follows me wherever I go. **Verse Ten: Both Man and Ox Forgotten** Both man and ox are forgotten; The traces of both are extinguished. In the vastness of empty space, There is neither subject nor object. **Verse Eleven: Returning Home** Returning home, I sit in peace; The gate is closed, and the world is forgotten. The moon shines through the window, And the spring breeze fills the courtyard. **Verse Twelve: Entering the City** Entering the city, I act with dignity; I carry the bowl and enter the marketplace. People see me and ask about my origins; I simply smile and do not speak. **Verse Thirteen: The Ox Forgotten** The ox is forgotten, and I am at ease; I wander freely through the world. I do not seek the tracks of the past; I do not cling to the present moment. **Verse Fourteen: The Ox Manifested** The ox is manifested, and I am joyful; I realize the nature of the Way. The ten directions are all within me; There is no place that is not the Way. **Verse Fifteen: The Ox Transcended** The ox is transcended, and I am liberated; I have attained the ultimate fruit. The myriad phenomena are all empty; Only the true mind remains. **Verse Sixteen: The Ox Perfected** The ox is perfected, and I am fulfilled; I have realized the great function. The universe is one with myself; There is no duality between us. **Verse Seventeen: The Ox Unfettered** The ox is unfettered, and I am free; I roam beyond the boundaries of the world. The clouds and mountains are my companions; The rivers and lakes are my home. **Verse Eighteen: The Ox Unbound** The ox is unbound, and I am at peace; I have cast off all constraints. The sun and moon are my lamps; The stars are my canopy. **Verse Nineteen: The Ox Unshackled** The ox is unshackled, and I am enlightened; I have awakened to the source of reality. The three realms are all empty; Only the Dharma-body remains. **Verse Twenty: The Ox Unconfined** The ox is unconfined, and I am sovereign; I have attained mastery over all things. The ten thousand dharmas are all one; There is no distinction between self and other. **Verse Twenty-One: The Ox Unobstructed** The ox is unobstructed, and I am unhindered; I pass through the gates of birth and death. The cycle of samsara is empty; Only nirvana remains. **Verse Twenty-Two: The Ox Unimpeded** The ox is unimpeded, and I am unattached; I dwell in the realm of non-action. The eight winds cannot move me; I am forever tranquil and still. **Verse Twenty-Three: The Ox Unconstrained** The ox is unconstrained, and I am unrestricted; I roam the ten directions without limit. The Great Way is vast and open; There is nowhere I cannot go. **Verse Twenty-Four: The Ox Unrestrained** The ox is unrestrained, and I am unburdened; I have cast off the weight of existence. The body is like a floating cloud; The mind is like the flowing water. **Verse Twenty-Five: The Ox Unbound** The ox is unbound, and I am liberated; I have attained the state of non-arising. All phenomena are originally empty; Only the true nature remains. **Verse Twenty-Six: The Ox Unfettered** The ox is unfettered, and I am free; I have transcended the realm of delusion. The six senses are all empty; Only the wisdom-mind remains. **Verse Twenty-Seven: The Ox Unconfined** The ox is unconfined, and I am sovereign; I have realized the nature of the Buddha. The three bodies are all one; There is no difference between them. **Verse Twenty-Eight: The Ox Unobstructed** The ox is unobstructed, and I am unhindered; I pass through the gates of the three worlds. Birth and death are like a dream; Only the eternal Dharma remains. **Verse Twenty-Nine: The Ox Unimpeded** The ox is unimpeded, and I am unattached; I dwell in the realm of non-discrimination. The ten thousand dharmas are all empty; Only the true mind remains. **Verse Thirty: The Ox Unconstrained** The ox is unconstrained, and I am unrestricted; I roam the ten directions without limit. The Great Way is vast and open; There is nowhere I cannot go. **Verse Thirty-One: The Ox Unrestrained** The ox is unrestrained, and I am unburdened; I have cast off the weight of existence. Not yet tamed, my hooves gallop on, undaunted by toil; East, west, south, and north, the paths are far and long, for I greedily crave fodder on level fields so vast.
I have forgotten my homeland, where the grass is of a different kind.
At first, though his nature was stubborn, his nostrils were already pierced; from then on, the cowherd boy lashed him with a painful whip.
With his entire body covered in blood and sweat, the thongs of the halter pulled taut, he strained with all his might as he gazed toward the distant mountains of home.
Restrained for a time, I emerge from the grass to rest from my galloping; I shall firmly follow this straw sandal wherever I go.
Everywhere the frost, dew, and clouds make the ground slippery; I dare not forget my weariness as I vigilantly subdue myself.
Turning its head, it does not pull at the straw rope; it turns its own head back. Its coat is white and its nature is already gentle;
it knows that water and grass are sufficient within the mountains. Though the cowherd has many intentions, he still leaves it tethered.
Tamed by the warm breeze under a bright sun, you follow my will with bowed head by the willow-lined stream;
Silently the flowers fall as the spring colors fade upon the plains; Let us return together, there is no need to lead you by the halter.
Unimpeded in subduing the mind for many years, it remains as it is; Neither by the water’s edge nor beneath the forest trees am I bound.
A single sound of the *qiang* flute rises with the pine wind; On this day, forgetting all concerns, there is more than enough joy.
Spontaneously, amidst the willow shade by the Hundred-Flower Brook, I eat my fill and lie upon the green turf with the clouds.
When the song has ended, the mountain boy has nothing more to do; Leaving his whip as a pillow, my sleep grows deep.
Forgetting all signs amidst the streams, mountains, clouds, and moonlight, The wooden man and the flowers and birds share the same intent;
The king’s water and grass have always been sufficient, As he strolls idly from west to east across the ponds and dikes.
The jade whip alone shines, the grass rope is useless and idle; No trace remains amidst the ancient paths.
Returning empty-handed alone beneath the forest moon, To take even one more step is to enter the iron gate.
Both vanish into the profound depths; neither man nor ox leaves a trace. A single orb of new moon illuminates the autumn sky.
If one asks within this for the principle of returning to the source: The wind falls upon the cliff-flowers, dotting the emerald thicket.
In Response to Master Bao’en’s Verses on the Chart of Taming the Ox (The Master’s name was Yuánxiū; his style name was Tiānyīn):

Before the ox is tamed, the waters and clouds stretch vast and wide, and the chaotic sounds of its bellowing resound. One must search for its tracks with meticulous care, yet the path grows ever more remote.
Day and night, amidst wind and frost, one knows not where it goes;
Fearing it will offend the family’s young sprouts, one first adjusts it, then seizes the rope-head and passes the nose-ring through. In vain does one apply further lashes to the very spot of pain.
One knows well that one's hometown is far away; turning the head back, one exerts effort to pull and restrain it.
It will not submit to being driven by its own nature from afar; held at every step, it wanders on and on.
How many times have black winds blown and torrential rains poured, Drenching my whole body in mud and water until all fatigue was forgotten?
Suddenly turning my head, I forgot all artifice; In silence, my nature and temperament became naturally supple and gentle.
In the mountains, one is fully content with water and grass; there is no need for hesitation or lingering abroad.
Tamed and submissive, roaming freely between woods and watersides, I ride crosswise upon my short flute, letting myself be at ease.
Returning home, a single expanse of misty clouds at evening; In carefree song and chant, there is no need for external constraints.
Entering and exiting without hindrance, the mind is as it is; Even where one attempts to deliberate, it remains further bound.
The man and the ox are at ease, filled with wind and moon; Whip and tether forgotten, there is more than enough joy.
Spontaneously amidst wild shores, stream bends, flowers, and willows, A single circuit of mountains and waters, lush with verdant forests.
Carefree and joyful, there is no seeking; With soft grass for a mat, the desire for sleep grows deep.
Forgetting all until one reaches the state of mindless oblivion— The ten thousand mountains are one color, utterly beyond comparison.
In the scenery where man and ox are not perceived, one moves spontaneously and freely from west to east;
shining alone,
there is no need for gathering or releasing, attaining a state of ease that transcends ordinary glances and gazes.
Strolling leisurely back beneath the bright moon, I tread upon and overturn both upper and lower barriers.
Where man and ox are both extinguished, no trace remains anywhere; The new moon hangs solitary, and the myriad phenomena are empty.

With horns towering high, he bellows forth; rushing along the misty waters, the path is far and long.
The cowherd has no lingering attachment to fodder or straw—who would dare to trespass upon the crops in the level fields at the start of their cultivation?
The ox’s nostrils have been pierced by a rope; Let it go or bring it back without the need for a whip.
Should it strike toward either the east or the west, Each time it enters the grass, it is pulled back again—thus constrained.
Years have passed and long days gone, weary of rushing and hurrying; Cloud shadows and stream reflections follow me wherever I go.
Though the flowers and birds of the imperial garden pass by, Their every song cannot call back the weary herder who turns his head.
Exhausted in strategy and at the limit of strength, he calls his head back; In vain he lets the whip and reins slacken.
Seven times released and eight times captured, he is bound beneath a tree; Yet the mountain boy still refuses to let him stay and tame him.
Amidst the mountains, beneath the forest trees, by the stream— Having eaten one’s fill, there is no further celebration;
with a sense of joyful liberation, the child lets go of the hand and returns as the path grows late. Without hindrance, he quickly leads the ox toward a distant village.
Sleeping peacefully in the open air, the mind is as it truly is; What can mirages or floating flowers constrain?
The mountain boy plays his iron flute with the resonance of pines; Gently blowing, he awakens one to a joy beyond compare, flowing spontaneously.
Moving freely through north, south, east, and west, The grass grows thick beneath my feet;
Having eaten my fill, only a trace of intention remains, Left for the mountain boy to slumber deeply in forgetfulness.
A single expanse of white like a cloud-bull— wherein could there be vermilion or difference? Within this,
if one seeks to distinguish the subtlest part, it moves and flows, drifting again toward the west and east, shining alone.
The cowherd boy claps his hands, naturally at ease; Only now does he believe the cow’s tracks have vanished from this place.
Thus he attains diligent joyfulness, Yet the stars and moon still remain to illuminate the secluded pass—both [subject and object] extinguished.
The man and the ox are completely extinguished, their traces utterly severed; Vast and expansive, the light swallows the void of the universe.

When the bright moon and the reeds come to inquire, The east wind blows them up in dense clusters. Chan Master Wanru (whose name was Tongwei) composed this verse in response to the *Ruminating Ox* illustrations: The man and the ox are completely extinguished, their traces utterly severed; Vast and expansive, the light swallows the void of the universe. When the bright moon and the reeds come to inquire, The east wind blows them up in dense clusters.
The unherded, base-natured, coarse, and wild ones flee outward; The homelands lie far away, yet they do not know it is distant.
Clearly, everywhere is a field of desolation; How could they be willing to turn their heads and cherish the rare sprouts?
At first, while taming him on the road, we met and passed through his nostrils; Even if he were of a wicked nature, we applied the whip with vigor.
From now on, the reins are firmly held in our hands; Should he wish to bolt at once, a single pull is enough.
Restrained for a time, the wildness briefly subsides; the galloping momentarily ceases. Frequently glancing back, they follow one another; though the guiding rope is slack, the whip still strikes.
One does not calculate the effort expended, nor does one begrudge the exhaustion.
Turning his head, the stubborn and unruly nature was eliminated; he looked back and, without applying further lashes or pressure, his disposition became gentle.
The cowherd did not dare to rely on his own will, but instead pulled tight on the end of the rope to keep him bound.
Tamed amidst the myriad trees and beside the fragrant grasses, The oxen release their tethering ropes, their minds serene.
Amidst the shadows of the setting sun, the crows caw as they return; The cattle follow one another naturally, with no need for a lead rope.
Unobstructed and pure white, his entire being is naturally as it is; The sea and sky are vast and wide, not constraining one another.
A cowherd boy leans idly against a rock by the pine tree; He blows his short flute repeatedly, his inspiration overflowing.
Spontaneously wandering by a thousand streams amidst ten thousand mountains, Eating and drinking as needed, satisfied among the lush green pastures;
Let the herder have no concerns at all, Snoring with his arm as a pillow, unaware of the depth of sleep.
Forgetting each other in this place, the ox is amidst the clouds and mountains; With neither thought nor intention, the moon shares its likeness with the azure sky.
As the shadow falls upon the rushing mountain stream, Let it wander freely to the west and to the east.
Shining alone upon my life, I have cast aside all worldly concerns and find my body at ease; The bright moonlight leaps forth among the ancient trees.
Having finished my song with a single cry, I return late in the evening; My straw sandals tread until worn through as I cross the barriers of my native land.
Both are extinguished, vast and empty, with no trace of either remaining; A precious moon hangs solitary, illuminating the azure sky.
There is no need to ask again about this matter: The cry of the cuckoo has ceased amidst the clusters of falling blossoms.
Chan Master Fushí of Dongtá (whose name was Tōngxián) composed a verse on the "Diagram of Herding an Ox":
Before being herded, one misses the single roar before sound; Consequently, biased views arise and the journey through the paths remains far.
Clad in fur and wearing horns, there is no concern at all; when was dung and grass ever known as the first sprouts of grain?
Only when first tamed does one realize the ox’s nose has already been pierced; yet, though it has suddenly consented, one still applies the whip with hardship.
Do not let the horse stray for even a moment; hold fast to the taut rein and guide it firmly.
Whether crossing waters or piercing through clouds, he gallops without confusion; Let him be called or sent as you wish, and he will always follow.
Though the calf is now fit for training, do not allow the mountain boy to let it rest even for a moment.
Each time it turns its head to enter the grass, it does so with a gentleness of nature that is already softened from its former state.
Petal-strewn paths evoke thoughts of treading upon them; amidst the mist and rain on the traveler’s road, how could one linger?
Tamed and submissive, I dwell beside ancient pines by the glistening rocks; letting events take their course with ease, I am finally at peace.
If there is a whip in your hand, you must let it go; if there is a rope in your nose, there is no need to pull.
When unimpeded, wherever you encounter him, you attain spontaneous ease; whether entering the mud or entering the water, why should you be constrained?
Eat when hungry, drink when thirsty, sleep when weary; in these matters, there has never been anything lacking or superfluous.
Let things proceed spontaneously, and your own eye opens wide within the universe: when a barbarian comes, he appears as a barbarian, letting him be as he is, thick and unruly.
The mountain boy sings idly a tune of returning home; Unconsciously, he causes the longing for one's origins to deepen.
Forgetting all, he has utterly cast away the thieving mind within his vast openness; What difference is there between man and ox, and what could they possibly share?
From now on, the power of both banks of the dike is severed; One may go west, one may go east.
Shining alone, having shed all skin and fur, the bare body is at ease; Magnificently revealed, it is present within a moment of laughter and talk.
It is not that these people are able to attain realization; It is simply because they have penetrated the ultimate barrier.
Both vanish, empty and silent, leaving no trace; A single point of spiritual mechanism is entirely swept away into voidness.

Wisdom’s principles do not abide, yet compassionate transformation is universal; A single bright moon illuminates the secluded thickets. The ox has always borne people, yet people do not recognize it; Why wander and leap about so far away?
Once one grasps the ox’s nose, Throughout the great chiliocosm, not a single blade of grass remains. This is the initial taming.
I address those who recognize the ox: do not follow the common crowd by forcefully lashing it with a whip.
"I am the ox, and the ox is me"—clearly there is no duality; how could such a thing be constrained or controlled?
The cowherd boy is not deluded by losing his head; His pure white ox follows him everywhere.
Unlike a merchant traveling on the road, He rides astride and strokes the beast at will, never wearying, as he turns his head back.
Do not say that one must turn their head only after long practice; The ox has no front or back, nor hardness or softness.
If the mountain boy but succeeds in stilling his wild mind, His nostrils will pervade the heavens, transcending both going and staying, tamed and submissive.
Those who are habitually busied with the trivial pursuits of the world may claim that only through long cultivation does one attain tranquility;
yet it is only upon seeing through this ox that there is no coming or going that one realizes how much time was wasted by such needless entanglement.
Unobstructed.
Primordially free and unbound, how could one who knows gratitude allow themselves to be forcibly constrained?
Flying and dancing in all directions without leaving a trace—who would believe that the *nāga*’s meditative absorption has any remainder? It proceeds spontaneously.
Making no distinction between inner and outer, or between the periphery and the center, I followed the fragrance by the water into the tangled thickets.
Turning my head, I saw the eastern mountains exhaling a new moon; Riding back to the thatched cottage, my inspiration remained intense— all things were forgotten.
Forcibly dividing the entire body into two parts—only when resources are exhausted and strength spent does one realize they are the same.
Cease all inquiries as to who is long and who is short; what need is there to speak of the person in the west and the object in the east? It is but solitary illumination.
Piercing the void with the crown and trampling the earth to dust, leaving not a single thing to clutter the space between;
though this solitary and towering state may seem enviable, it is only upon a sudden flash of shame that one truly penetrates the barrier— where both [subject and object] vanish.
Who is the one being herded? Who is the herder? Recognizing shadows and trailing after the wind—it is utterly empty.
If you ask for the essential meaning within this, You would have known long ago that straw dogs bark at reed thickets.
Chan Master Ru’An (whose name was Tongwen) composed these verses on the Herding Ox Diagram.
The untrained herdsman roams the ends of the earth, bellowing at will; Traversing clouds and crossing waters, his path is long and arduous.
For many years he has possessed this vast field of leisure, Yet his trampling is pitiable, as it destroys the ripening grain.
At first, the nostrils were difficult to tame and hard to pierce; once it had entered the grass, one must apply the whip.
What stratagem could ever bind this wild mind? It relies on the mountain boy to pull it with the rope.
Bound and constrained, where else could you possibly gallop? Dusk rains and morning mists closely follow your tracks;
Though you seek to flee and hide, No matter how fiercely you run, you shall only grow weary.
Turning my head, I suddenly find consent within myself and look back; The ground is covered with fallen red petals, soft against the grass.
With lingering thoughts for my native land, my feelings cannot be cast aside; I harbor a silent sorrow that spring is fading, yet still lingers on.
Tamed and brought back, then released by the ancient stream; wind and moon follow conditions, naturally silent.
Without a bottomless matter to contemplate regarding water and grass, we gaze at one another, letting go of hands and forgetting the tether.
Unimpeded strides through streams and mountains, moving with ease; Wind and elegance on both banks—what constraints could there be?
Blowing the short flute crosswise at the close of the setting sun, The springtime radiance overflowing the eyes is truly abundant.
Spontaneously,
he has never moved a step beyond the mountains; amidst the warm clusters of bright flowers and five-colored tufts of grass,
do not wonder at the mountain boy’s idle dozing— their delight in reclining upon clouds and sleeping beneath the moon is particularly profound.
Forgetting one another and walking together in the peace of non-action—how utterly different is this from my own state of mind!
All fragments of idleness and sorrow are gathered up; I know not where the flowers fall or the waters flow eastward.
Shining alone upon the single path of cold light, ten thousand realms are at ease; Vastly and silently, the four eyes gaze upon the waters and clouds.
After the bright moon has returned at night’s depth, It shines through to the ultimate barrier of the Sovereign of Emptiness.
Both vanish;
seeking their traces from before, not a shadow remains. Neither person nor ox is seen; mist and waters are empty.
The entire earth returns to the dawn of spring; as the sun rises high, fragrance disperses through the clusters of a hundred flowers.
Chan Master Shanzu’s Verse on the Diagram of Herding the Ox (the Master’s name was Tongji):
Before the ox is tamed, it roams at will by the waterside and grassy banks, bellowing; With no halter upon its nose, it wanders far away.
Who would have known that the entire universe is transformed by the King’s influence? Yet they trample through clouds and mountains, violating the ripening grain.
First adjusting the hemp rope, first grasping the nose-ring to lead it through— Where one is accustomed, it is hard to forget; one must strike with the whip with painful urgency.
Entrust the cowherd boy with firm protection; do not let him for a moment lose the lead held in his hand.
Restraint moves the body, yet the stubborn nature loves to gallop; as he turns his eyes left and right, the calf follows closely behind.
Gazing longingly at the distant mountains, news from home is lost; Clad in clouds and girded by the moon, I am truly free from weariness.
Turning my head, I recognize my debt of gratitude; with every step, I am willing to look back. My fierce temper has melted away, and my nature gradually becomes supple.
Riding toward level slopes and deep grass, he plays his short flute with unrestrained freedom; Tamed and submissive,
he stays by the willows along the plains, where the rider casts aside the whip and reins and sits in tranquil ease.
The evening mountain bells toll as the moon rises above; returning thus, there is no need for guidance.
The man and the ox gaze at each other without obstruction, their essence in a state of suchness. Since both are without mind, there is no need for constraint.
Wandering at will amidst the clusters of flowers and willows, His hoofprints circle round with nothing left behind;
Moving spontaneously, sometimes through villages, sometimes among the clouds, Upon old grounds and fallow fields, the grass is lush and green.
Traversing all things until not a trace remains, The cowherd lies high-sleeping beneath the thick willow shade.
Forgetting all worldly concerns, he rests with head uplifted in the forest; He and I have utterly forgotten our shared life as cloud-dwellers and water-folk.
For the sake of love, the meadow grass before the mountain is fine; Deep in the night, riding the moonlight, one crosses to the east of the stream.
The scenery within this very self shines alone all day long; Relaxing the body, one lies peacefully amidst the white clouds.
A single long song, its sound clear and resonant, Pierces straight through the barrier beyond the kalpa of Wei-yin.
Both man and ox vanish; not even a trace remains. The pure wind and bright moon fill the vast expanse of space.
In an era of Great Peace, there is no need to sing the edicts of Yao; The withered tree once again blooms with a cluster of flowers.

Master Tongyuean (whose name was Miaoyong and whose style name was Xuanwei) composed verses on the "Diagram of Tending the Ox" (in response to the verse on the stage of "Not Yet Tended"). **Not Yet Tended:** In an era of Great Peace, there is no need to sing the edicts of Yao; The withered tree once again blooms with a cluster of flowers. *Note: The final line of the original text, "Tongyuean Dashi he muniu tu song," indicates that Master Tongyuean composed these verses on the "Diagram of Tending the Ox. The preceding lines constitute the first stage of the ox-herding sequence, "Not Yet Tended," as adapted by the master.*
A roar from beneath the low-hanging black clouds—how could one have known the distance of the path beneath one's feet?
At that moment, the youth took up the *guansuo* noose; he had never before paid heed to cherishing the fine sprouts, for he was but newly trained.
The nostrils have only today begun to be pierced; This ten-fold wild nature deserves only the whip.
To make him understand ordinary matters, One must disregard the pull of his entire body’s black karma.
The paths today do not lead one astray; The whip and reins follow gently as I go.
Hills, streams, water, and grass are provided at will; Walking freely in this elegant manner, I am never weary.
Turning my head back...
Beside the green willow embankment, at the head of the azure stream, the scenery is naturally bright and harmonious, and the breeze is naturally gentle.
The water buffalo turns its head and consents; on the moonlit path home, there is no need for lingering delay.
Tamed and submissive.
Coming from there, passing over here; turning left and circling right, all is at ease.
The yellow oriole calls and the mountain flowers bloom; amidst sounds and forms, one is not led astray—unimpeded.
Detached from emptiness, the myriad phenomena are as they are; Man and ox roam freely, unrestrained by one another.
The whip and reins cast down, not a trace remains; To stir the spirit, a single tune of plum blossoms lingers—let things follow their natural course.
I remain at ease within a single awakening, letting them wander along grassy paths among the fine tufts of vegetation;
as the evening sun sets on the spring mountains where fallen flowers bury one's knees, the crimson clouds are still drenched in the dense richness of brocade— thus we forget ourselves.
White clouds sweep across the midst of the bright moon; The moon and the clouds are of one and the same color.
In this realm of wisdom, nothing is perceived at all; What need is there to discuss south, north, west, or east?
It shines alone.
The household is ruined and desolate within the four walls; now, amidst the clarity of clouds and the brightness of the moon, this is certainly no longer a matter of the ordinary path.
It is better to press forward with one's whole being and pass through the barrier, where both [subject and object] are utterly extinguished.
The drama has ended; where can one seek its traces? One should not carve emptiness within the void.
Who could say it is revealed in its full majesty? Bees and butterflies are deluded amidst the clusters of flowers.
A Verse on the Ox-Herding Pictures by Master Zhizhi An (the master’s name was Minghai, his style name was Xiangdang).
Unherded, it rushes east and west, letting loose wild roars; Crossing ridges and winding through streams, it knows no dread of distance.
With eyes fixed only on the weeds by the field’s edge, It knows not that, if it turns its head, there is the sacred sprout.
For how many years at first did you train, your nostrils never yet pierced? Today you have been brought back and finally whipped;
the lead-rope is held firm without the slightest slackening—each time he enters the weeds, he is pulled back once more.
Restrained by his stubborn hide, he delights in ceasing his gallop; I walk by the stream and he follows me.
Only fearing that the willow threads cannot hold him fast, He watches over me with tireless diligence.
Turning my head back, I have brought this one ox home by myself; How many times did I test its strength and suppleness with whip and staff?
Now that I have trodden the path back to my own home, I am too weary to listen to the yellow orioles on the branches.
Tamed and submissive by several low slopes and shallow waters, they dwell together in harmonious intimacy, their spirits filled with contentment.
As the mountain clouds gather at dusk, they return to the village; they follow their keepers with such grace that no leading rope is required.
Unimpeded by water or grass, ordinary affairs proceed as they may; Let them drink and peck as they please, for I am too weary to constrain them.
The sound of the flute awakens the coral moon; Only a single point of its pure radiance remains in disarray.
Strolling at ease across the level foothills of the spring mountains, where the breeze is gentle, the sun warm, and the grasses lush,
I sleep soundly upon a pillow of vines and stones, unconcerned whether the colors of the cliff flowers are pale or deep.
Mutually forgetting, the entire body is pure and bright amidst a single cloud; The bright moon and the reeds do not permit companionship.
Though it is said the jade tower windows have already dawned, The golden sun remains still over the eastern sea-gate.
Shining alone upon the ox, it is empty by itself and the person is naturally at ease; Tranquil and solitary, one walks between water and clouds.
Yet one must still suddenly turn the body over— To topple the final barrier at the end of the road.
Both skin and hair, raincoat and hat, have vanished without a trace; A single expanse of cold light falls into the azure sky.
News of the old garden is cut off by mist and rain; Where among the myriad flowers can one hear the fragrance of the clusters?
A Carriage Crushing the Wayfarer: A Verse on the "Diagram of Taming the Ox" by Grand Councilor Yan Dahe Before the Ox is Tamed:
Amidst the mountain clouds, a single roar; The horns and head are distinct, yet the home message remains far away.
Having traversed every idle flower across the ground, who would have known there were strange weeds and fine sprouts?
At first, it was as wild and fierce as a tiger’s snout, difficult to pierce; yet, fortunately, the cowherd boy possessed a rope and a whip.
It was not a single application of a sharp hand; at such a time, a base nature is difficult to restrain.
The familiar path is hard to forget as one seeks to gallop forth; the thorny rope remains in hand, following closely behind.
How could one allow oneself to chase after grass and seek out fragrances? Day and night, one restrains and binds [the mind], undaunted by fatigue.
If one turns back for a moment and falls into the weeds, The clouds will freeze, the frost will chill, and the feet will already be numbed.
Though one wishes to loosen the whip’s lash, it remains yet untethered; As the homelands remain out of reach, they are detained and held fast.
Tamed and submissive upon high and deep paths, winding and boundless, Through mutual restraint and training, their docility is now assured.
In the shade of willows, the crimson sun turns its course; the rope on the tip of the nose has snapped—there is no need to pull it.
With unimpeded water and grass, even emperors and kings are entirely at ease; why must one needlessly constrain them with such hardship?
The mountain boy lets go and sits high first; the ox, too, is at ease with plenty of leisure.
Walking freely and following one's faith, they arrive here where the grass is lush before and behind the mountain.
Let him loose to roam and wander among the ponds and dikes; He is no longer like those days when his wild enthusiasm was thick.
In this atmosphere of peace and forgetting, amidst the bright moonlight, Your home and my mountain—every color and form are the same.
With hands folded and brows lowered, I forget my office; I know not whether going west or coming east.
Traces solitary, alone and at ease; In this state of total integration, what room is there for "coming" or "going"?
Singing and chanting alone beneath the empty mountains, how many deluded people mistake this for passing through the barrier!
To speak of the ox and man both vanishing as a mere "extinction of traces" is no different from blowing on the wind hoping to fill the void.
If one asks about the intent of returning to the source and reaching the intimate essence, the thorny brambles piercing the heavens grow in dense clusters;
the Ox-Cart driver treads over them once more as he chants his verses on the "Chart of Taming the Ox," beginning with "The Untamed."
The sound "mou mou" is his roar; if you seek the trace of his head, it recedes further and further.
Meeting him on the narrow path, you finally recognize him; willing to endure hunger, he does not taste the sprouts at first.
The Mother’s nostrils have never been pierced; Where it hurts, needles and awls sting, where it hurts, the whip lashes.
One might say the cowherd has laid a poisoned hand upon him, Fearing that if he were allowed to run wild, he would pull even harder at the reins.
The ancient road is desolate; why do you hasten along it? The paths of other mountains are winding and crooked—would they truly follow you?
Foolish children do not let go of the rope’s end; They bind empty space tightly, only to exhaust themselves in vain.
Turn your head back!
Since treading this source, though its bone-strength is firm, its coat-color is supple;
as the sun thins toward the Yu-yuan abyss, its intent to return is urgent—how could it greedily linger over fodder and grass? Thus it remains docile and submissive.
Circled hoofprints by the ancient shore; Feeding when hungry and drinking when thirsty, they roam at ease.
Coming from the east and going to the west, all is level and smooth; Leaving home and returning, they are never bound—unimpeded.
At the head of the ridge and by the stream, all is as it is; Whether walking upright or sleeping crosswise, there is no further constraint.
The King of Water and Grass provides according to his means; Originally there is neither lack nor excess—let things proceed spontaneously.
The oxen roam at leisure within these mountains; They lie upon the grass and sleep amidst the flowers, satiated by the lush greenery.
From of old, they have never entered the narrow paths of the world; In their carefree and independent state, their joy is all the more profound as they forget all else.
Man and ox dwell together amidst the green crags; everywhere, the streams, mountains, clouds, and moon are one.
Monkeys and birds cry out of their own accord, flowers bloom by themselves; the water flows westward while the bank shifts east, illuminating all alone.
Having shed all skin and fur, one attains spontaneous leisure; Tranquil and solitary, one walks alone amidst the waters and clouds.
Pity those infinite men of heroic spirit— With eyes wide open, they solemnly enter the barrier of death, where both [subject and object] vanish.
Meeting him everywhere, yet leaving no trace; the azure sky is clear and the lunar orb is empty.
How many traces of refined elegance dwell within this! The incense of the precious duck has faded amidst the brocade clusters.
This is the third song of the Herding the Ox series by the Wayfarer [Chandu].
Before being herded, the primordial body and nature suddenly let out a roar; shaking the earth and startling the heavens, its function is not remote.
Having chewed through mountain flowers and sucked dry the waters, it leaves behind not a single stalk of the permanent abiding.
At first, the nostrils were adjusted to point toward heaven, refusing to be pierced; who could bring themselves to lay a hand upon them and rashly apply the whip?
Though the cowherd may still hold the end of the rope, it is a waste of effort to pull with such force.
The ox, though constrained, drives its own feet along; It is laughable that the blind man follows step by step through mud and water.
The deep stream is utterly unstained; Leading him into the grass—will he not grow weary?
Turning the head, twisting the neck, and circling the hooves, one loses the way; What distinction can there be between the stubborn and the weak, or the hard and the soft?
Suddenly go straight home; There is no need to linger abroad.
Tamed and at ease, he roams by the stream and among the grass; whether to mount or dismount, he remains perfectly at peace.
With the tethering rope coiled upon his head, he makes his home wherever he goes, needing no longer to be led.
Everywhere the streets are like those of unimpeded willows and cypress flowers; what restriction is there for one who violates the crops?
Charging straight through and colliding sideways, all is unimpeded; the old molds are overturned without remainder.
Spontaneously returning at midnight when the moon is at its zenith, The grass grows thick upon the Three-Life Stone.
In this era of Great Peace, there is no need to slay the dull-witted and stubborn; Let them do as they please, blowing their iron flutes with all their might.
Mutually forgetting [the man and the ox] within this very midst—black and white have always been of one identical color.
I am not like him, yet he is like me; who can distinguish north from south or east from west?
Shining alone upon the herdsman, he never ceases from tending to dung and urine;
With a lash toward the Unborn, in the blink of an eye, when the spirit is high, let the spirit swell further— What need to hesitate? A single arrow shall shatter the three barriers.
The pair vanish;
the mud ox enters the sea, leaving no trace. The wooden horse neighs in the wind toward the azure sky.
How can this matter be further discussed? Flowers bloom upon the iron tree in dense profusion.

The Lame Monk’s Verse on the Diagram of Herding an Ox (with Preface) From the time the Buddhas manifested their traces until the Patriarch came from the West, there has been nothing but the elucidation of this very matter. Whether by raising the fist, brandishing the whisk, administering the hot stick, or shouting the hot roar, they solely upheld the upward-turning wheel of the ultimate pivot.
Master Chan Puming, borrowing the metaphor of a person and a method, has once again established the Diagram of Herding an Ox.
Verse: The *chùduò* (cart) rolls over the layman to repay the Buddha’s kindness; He restores the ancestral Buddhas’ site of enlightenment. The Great Chan Master adds flowers upon brocade;
This lame man paints the eyes upon the dragon. The wind and moon of Chang’an pierce through past and present;
Which man among men would not be a true hero? A-he-he! What a fine brother!
Unherded, its horns fierce and formidable, it bellows at will; Having traversed the distant paths of mountain and stream,
If the cowherd does not pass the nose-rope through its nostrils, One cannot guarantee that its wild mind will not trample the young sprouts.
At first, adjust the head-rope held in your hand and pass it through the nose-ring; If its nature is base and difficult to tame, apply the whip firmly.
From this point on, do not slacken for even a moment; The cowherd must surely lead it with frequent pulling.
Bound by inferior natures, the mind’s restlessness is gradually stilled; led step by step, it follows along.
Even as the cowherd boy continues to exert his spirit, reaching this state, he is entirely unaware of fatigue.
Turning back the head, when the wild and frantic mind is exhausted, one finally turns around; through uninterrupted application, the ox becomes naturally docile.
Guided by hand back beneath the bright moon, it is spared from lingering among water and grass.
Tamed and submissive, whether by mountain or by water, Clearly free from affairs, one is naturally at ease.
The myriad phenomena of the universe are but trivial matters; From now on, there is no need to lead the ox.
Unobstructed and uniquely manifest, the noble spirit remains at ease; Sleeping peacefully or sitting steadily, one is already free from constraints.
The cowherd boy idly picks up his short flute to play; With a single horizontal blast, his joy is more than sufficient.

Spontaneously, consciousness breaks through to realize that it has always been within this very midst; Wildflowers and weeds grow lush as they please, with no obstruction from east, west, south, or north;
Clapping hands and singing aloud, my inspiration is at its peak.
The illusory white ox is imagined to dwell only within the white clouds; whether drinking from thirst or eating from hunger, it is always the same.
The mountain boy stands idly upon the rock—here, why inquire further of east or west?
Shining alone upon the ox where no tracks remain, all is tranquil; The full moon is perfectly round right here.
Naturally possessed are a pair of hands for the destitute; With a single blow, one passes straight through ten thousand layers of barriers.
Both man and ox vanish together, leaving no trace in the profound stillness; Water flows in the long river, the moon hangs in the void.
The monkey carries its young back to the green peaks; The bird holds a falling flower in its beak amidst the emerald crags.
A Verse on the "Diagram of the Herdsman Tending Cattle" by the Independent Wayman Xu Hui Changzhi (style name: Jinzhou):
Before the ox has been herded, its horns have not yet emerged; with a single roar, it wanders freely and unrestrained across distant paths.
Black and white are first distinguished as male and female; born with a gentle and compliant nature, the spiritual sprout has long been well-tamed.
Today it receives its piercing; why need the youth trouble himself by adding lashes?
With the clue in hand, turning at any moment, Everywhere the scenery is free from attachment or constraint.
Treading upon the streams and mountains, one gallops forth; Morning travel and evening lodging follow closely behind.
Each time it drinks water, its belly swells; It carries its burden steadily, never wearying.
To look back is truly pitiable—its fierce nature knows no turning back; Fortunately, it was born with a naturally gentle disposition.
Flowers fall everywhere across the world, yet one forgets where they tread; On the traveler's path through mist and clouds, do not linger.
Tamed and submissive, making no distinction between inner and outer, center and periphery; Bound yet unrestrained, the mind is utterly free and serene.
Walking at ease along the path, all is level ground; Flowing freely and spontaneously, there is no attachment and no hindrance.
Though phenomena differ in myriad ways, their nature is fundamentally such; Transcending the crowd, this nature alone is without constraint.
Bearing the entire burden with all one's might, In one’s fundamental nature, how could there ever be any lack? Leaving things to their natural course,
for a moment resting the shoulders and lying amidst the clouds, Suddenly, new sprouts emerge, lush with the vitality of life.
Carrying weight and traveling far, at ease according to one's will; Within this, walking alone, one’s joy is especially deep.
Forgetting each other and suddenly forgetting all mental control within the great void, Thirsty they drink and hungry they eat, the same everywhere.
When both self and objects are utterly relinquished, conceptual understanding is purified; Like the sun rising in the west and setting in the east,
one shines alone, attaining a place of peace and leisure— peaceful and at ease, leaving no tracks behind in the human world.
In a fleeting glance, brilliant wisdom and clear understanding are attained;
The barrier of silver mountains and iron walls is kicked down, both vanish, and the pure hearing beyond the wall is utterly traceless. Form and shadow, solitary and cold, reflect upon the azure void.
The window frames have already passed; there is nothing at all. Furthermore, what of the herdsman and the path of men amidst the clusters of bamboo in the vihāra?
This is a verse by Xiang Zhenben and He Mugu on the "Diagram of Herding Oxen," titled "Before Herding."
Amidst green mountains and blue waters, one roars at will; looking in the four directions, the path turns far away in three circuits.
One merely hastens along, greedy for speed, unaware that in daily life one is violating the fine sprouts of the initial cultivation.
As soon as the ox is seen, its nose is pierced through; The coarse and floating habitual tendencies are urgently whipped.
At that time, when it stubbornly resists and bolts away, One must firmly hold the head-rope and pull it back with force to bring it under control.
The four hooves have now ceased their galloping; Whether released or gathered back, they follow without fail.
How joyful it is that the whip and reins are still held in hand— Why would the cowherd boy grow weary of himself?
He turns his head.
Having traversed the mountain streams until one turns back, when the familiar becomes strange, the nature gradually softens.
A single thread passes through the nose—this is the matter accomplished; there is no need for the strength of the wrist to detain it for a moment as it becomes tamed and submissive.
Turning left and circling right by the emerald stream, I cast aside the whip’s cord and delight in spontaneity.
Time and again beneath the green willows returning under the night moon, The mountain boy sleeps soundly, having forgotten to pull the tether—
unimpeded.
Wagging his tail and holding his head high, he is perfectly at ease; Moving freely and without constraint, what need is there for restriction?
Leisurely, a single melody resounds upon a cold cliff; The short flute blows open the remnants beyond the mundane world—let things take their own course.
When hungry, eat; when thirsty, drink—cutting off both extremes and the middle. When weary, simply lie down with the clouds upon the lush grass.
Let one’s swift strides be left to the green peaks beyond; the兴致 (xìngzhì—spiritual interest) for wind and moon fills the breast, growing ever more intense as all distinctions are forgotten.
Man and ox dwell together in this mountain; their movements and actions are utterly beyond distinction.
I am originally he, and he is myself; we do not know south, north, west, or east—shining alone.
The ox has no fixed place, and the cowherd is at leisure; He lazily refuses to let empty fame fall into the world.
Though the entire earth comes seeking me, there is no "I" to be found; Without even a snap of the fingers, he passes through the heavy barrier—both vanish.
When both man and ox are exhausted, all traces vanish; Past and present respond to one another, and even kalpas are empty.
The local scenery of the original ground is a single matter: In the cold of winter, the pines and cypresses remain lush and verdant.
Chan Master Juchie (whose name was Jixian) composed this verse in response to the "Chart of Tending the Ox."

Unherded, the wild ones run loose, relying on their inferiority to display their roars; Suddenly separated from home by a distance of a hundred thousand miles, the traveler’s road is vast and the clouds and mist are black;
The weeds of ignorance grow long, obscuring the sprouts of the numinous mind.
At first you were wild and unbridled, now you are accustomed to being led; Bound by the rope once, you have been dragged with the whip many times.
Slogging through mud and water, forgetting dawn and dusk, The pain pierces to the core of my heart as I pull you with all my might.
Restrained and firmly held by the tether, it is forbidden from galloping astray; At every step and every stay, it follows closely behind.
In all actions and movements, it relies entirely upon its strength; From this point on, the mind and spirit shall never again grow weary.
Turning the head back, one is bound to the previous state; The inferior nature dissolves into waves of gentle light and the passing of fragrant breezes.
By the willow banks and flowering streams, one remains with joyful intent.
Tamed and serene amidst the remnants of mountains and waters, Moving freely and gathering at will, all is tranquil.
The path home is broad and unobstructed; Whatever the heart desires, it is not entangled.
Unobstructed, like the moonlight and breeze after a clearing rain, he dwells in tranquil ease; what thing could possibly restrain him while his ox rests?
Under the tall pines, the mountain boy sits with legs spread wide; a single tune from the flute of non-arising still lingers.
Spontaneously at ease, unbound by existence or non-existence;
Spontaneously partaking of the empty greenery, wild birds vie in song and flowers vie in laughter; The profound flavor of deep slumber upon the stone.
Mutually forgetting,
the pure white ox remains entirely within this; completely forgetting you and me, we are fundamentally one with the streams and mountains,
which can be gazed upon from every place— unrestricted by north or south, west or east.
Shining alone upon one’s life, vast and penetrating, he sells his leisure; Empty-handed yet held high, he has arrived at this very place.
With a mouth full of words, it is difficult to repay this incomparable price; How many have purchased passage through the barrier before the kalpa?
Both vanish as light is concealed and traces are obscured, leaving no lingering footprints; man and ox merge as two in the infinite void.
Beyond the kalpas, the fragrant breeze flows eternally—do not let bees or butterflies mistake it for a cluster of flowers.
Chan Master Juchech’s Verse on the Painting of the White Ox (the Master’s name was Jixian) The Ox Lost “The white ox is in the west; the boy is in the east.
The ox still seeks the ox, and the boy still seeks the boy; The boy and the ox face each other, one toward the west and one toward the east.”
Not a speck of dust can separate them—how vast the difference between heaven and earth! From beginningless kalpas until now, you have vainly remained in ignorance.
(The Master asks the boy where the ox is; the boy is utterly bewildered and at a loss. Then another person comes from the west and points with his hand toward the distance.
Suddenly he asks the mountain boy about the white ox; the mountain boy is perplexed and does not know how to seek it.
A bystander recognizes the ox’s tracks, pointing them out;
the mountain boy quickly turns his head to see the traces (the boy runs swiftly toward the west; many ox tracks are seen in the fields).
The embankment curves back and the path turns toward the western stream; along the way, deep hoofprints alternate with shallow ones.
Seeking old acquaintances through new knowledge, Man and ox, having reached this point, are both free from delusion.

Seeing the Ox (the white ox lies peacefully in the field; the youth sees it from afar and rejoices), Having traversed the mountain villages, he passes through the water villages; Suddenly, amidst the grass, he sees the white ox crouching.
Joyfully and with steady steps, he moves with light ease; his breath is first regulated as they discuss in detail.
Having found the ox (the white ox rising calmly, the youth joyfully pats its back), traversing streams and mountains, how could he dread the toil?
Having suddenly obtained the white ox, its value is all the more high.
In our long separation, our hearts have rejoined; with gentle care and composure, we joyfully lay aside our armor.
(The youth sits idly upon the rock; the white ox drinks from the stream, content.
The ox is at ease while the man grows thin; with the wind clear and the moon bright, hunger is long forgotten.
Mysterious fragrance and wild greens fill the valleys; How many times have the morning and evening suns shone upon them?

Returning on horseback (the setting sun rests on the mountain; the white ox returns to its lodging; the boy rides upon the ox’s back, playing the flute for his own delight), This carefree return on horseback is rare in this world.
The willow-branch whip casts shadows as it is swung by the wind.
The mountain boy blows the flute to the end of the "Song of Non-arising," Its melodic resonance follows the fading light into the imperial palace.
Having forgotten the ox, the white cow is entirely lost with no trace remaining;
The wild and reckless cowherd whistles atop the solitary peak.
Mountains and rivers are reflected upside down as the moon turns;
Jade dew is cool and clear, light and shadow both vanish (man and ox are both unseen; there is only one perfect circle).
Layer upon layer of pavilions open at the snap of a finger; Originally there is neither lack nor excess—the seven kinds of wealth.
Vainly transmitted through fifty-three houses of infamy, The man and the ox vanish; the great dream returns.

Entering the marketplace (the youth walks forward toward the east, while the white ox follows behind), He flaunts his leisurely white ox, Entering the marketplace with hands hanging down, roaming at will.
The compassionate breeze flows equally through the nine realms; there is no distinction to be sought between mind, Buddha, and sentient beings.
